column5: 1948 election (26/05/1948): NP and Afrikaner Party won 79 seats to the United Party's 65, Labour 6 and three Native Representatives: a majority of five. Welsh stresses Afrikaner unity as the underlying cause. Course lesson 1 says the 'National Party's 1948 victory' without detail: add the narrow margin

Course: Natives Land Act 1913 'confined most Africans to a small share of the land'. Welsh: it prevented Africans buying land outside scheduled reserves and passed with hardly any dissent, because a cross-party consensus on segregation existed at Union and for over a decade after. So apartheid after 1948 built on a bipartisan segregation, and colour policy only became a party-political fight from 1929 (swart gevaar campaign). Add this to Module 5 lesson 1

Hertzog tried from 1926 to remove the Cape's African male voters from the common roll, achieved in 1936 (Welsh signals this in chapter 1); the 1922 Rand strike cost over 150 lives; Boer War camps: estimated 28,000 women and children died. Background for lesson 1 on foundations

Welsh: the word 'apartheid' entered official NP terminology in 1944; urban African numbers rose 57 per cent between 1936 and 1946 as wartime industry suspended pass-law enforcement, which NP politicians called 'swamping'; Smuts admitted in 1942 that segregation had failed to stop urbanisation. Origin story for Module 5 lesson 1: apartheid was a reaction to urbanisation and a pre-existing segregation, not a bolt from nowhere

1948 election: UP-Labour won about 53.3 per cent of votes against 39.4 per cent for the NP-AP (Heard's estimate, quoted by Welsh) but fewer seats, because of the first-past-the-post system and rural over-representation. A strong 'figures' item for Module 5 lesson 1: the government that began apartheid won a seat majority of five with a minority of the vote; Welsh adds that Afrikaner unity and 'black peril' campaigning fused as causes

Debate: was apartheid a blueprint? The NP's Sauer Commission report (March 1948) had about 30 concrete proposals nearly all enacted within a decade, but Cillie and Posel argue implementation was pragmatic and piecemeal (Minister Jansen admitted in August 1948 the method for industries and towns was 'still to be worked out'); Welsh thinks the core intent (baasskap, curbing urbanisation, removing Coloured vote) was set before 1948. Good for a 'Historians disagree' mini-table in lesson 1; also Welsh gives the NP aim as shoring up white domination, not only separate development

Course: 'The Natives Land Act of 1913 confined most Africans to a small share of the land' and 'ANC was founded in 1912'. Welsh gives numbers: the 1913 Act scheduled about 7 per cent of the land surface as reserves; the Native Trust and Land Act of 1936 released a further 7.25 million morgen, bringing African-held or trust land to 17.75 million morgen, 13.7 per cent of the land surface. Also the body founded at Bloemfontein in 1912 was the South African Native National Congress; the name ANC dates from 1925. Add the figures and the name to lesson 1

Urban African population grew 94.49 per cent 1921-36 and 57.16 per cent 1936-46; by 1946 about 1.794 million urban Africans (23 per cent of Africans), more than the white urban population by about 75,000. Pass laws served to tie workers to employers and allocate labour. W. M. Macmillan 1930: Africans living on one-fifth of land they once claimed. The Cape non-racial male franchise: 7.5 per cent of Cape electorate African by 1929, abolished for Africans in 1936 with only 11 MPs voting against. Background for Module 5 lesson 1 (foundations)

Pre-1948 African politics in Welsh: ICU under Clements Kadalie (claimed 100,000 members in 1927), ANC Youth League formed 1944 (Mandela, Tambo, Sisulu, Lembede), ANC's 'Africans' Claims in South Africa' 1943, Programme of Action adopted December 1949 (boycott, strike, civil disobedience), 1946 African miners' strike with about 60,000 participants brutally broken, PAC founded 1959 after the 1958 Africanist breakaway. Lesson 2 (resistance) starts at the 1952 Defiance Campaign; add one paragraph on the 1940s roots

Welsh stresses continuity: 1948 South Africa was already 'comprehensively racialised and segregated'; apartheid extended existing institutions more ruthlessly and under an ideology of nationalism and religion. Useful framing sentence for lesson 1; also Mandela quoted on his own 1940s African-nationalist anti-communism (a nuance for the 'Mandela' image)

Lembede (1940s) named 'psychological enslavement' and the 'Ja-Baas' mentality; Welsh traces the line from Lembede to Biko's Black Consciousness ('colonisation of the mind'), and notes each generation (1940s Youth League, late 1950s Africanists/PAC, late 1960s-70s BC students) was more impatient. Gives the Biko/Lecturer lens a root; use in lesson 2 (Biko) and the barrier aid

Population Registration Act 1950 and Group Areas Act 1950 confirmed as pillars; Welsh quotes Slabbert that the Population Registration Act underlay racial privilege in jobs, land, schools and housing. Course table is right on both years

Group Areas removals to 31/08/1984: 83,691 Coloured, 40,067 Indian and 2,418 white families (Welsh). Coloured common-roll vote ended 1956 (Separate Representation of Voters Act, after packing the Senate and the Appellate Division). Job reservation under the 1956 Industrial Conciliation Act amendment. Section 10 of the Native (Urban Areas) Act: an African could stay in a proclaimed urban area beyond 72 hours only with birth, 10 years' one employer or 15 years' residence, family tie or permit; reference books for women from 1956 and full influx control for women from 1963. Material for the 'laws' table and a pass-law worked example in lesson 1

Welsh's three phases of apartheid: 1948 to 1959 entrenching power (Malan, Strijdom), 1959 to 1966 'separate development' (Verwoerd), from 1966 erosion. The Tomlinson Commission (1955) projected for the year 2000 about 21.36 million Africans and 4.58 million whites, and that even with reserves holding 70 per cent of Africans some 6.5 million would stay in 'white' areas: Verwoerd rejected its main proposals. This is a demographic argument for why apartheid was unworkable; add to lesson 4 (why it ended) as a structural cause the course lacks

Bantu Education Act 1953 and Bantustan policy 'from 1959' (Promotion of Bantu Self-Government Act, 1959) both confirmed; Welsh also dates the earlier Bantu Authorities Act to 1951 (chiefs as fulcrum), so 'from 1959' is the self-government statute, not the first homeland law

Bantu Education: per-pupil spending 1953 R127.84 white versus R17.08 African; 1969-70 R282.00 versus R16.97 (about 16 to 1). Homeland 'independence': Transkei 1976, Bophuthatswana 1977, Venda 1979, Ciskei 1981, stripping over eight million of South African citizenship; the Surplus People Project estimated 3.5 million (about 10 per cent of the population) were forcibly removed by 1983; KwaZulu was 29 blocks and the nine homelands 91 blocks. 6.5 million prosecutions for pass offences 1946 to 1964/5 (Savage). Numbers for the laws table and a worked example

Welsh gives Sharpeville as '69 Africans killed by police on 21 March 1960' during a pass-law protest (he uses the official count; he does not give the 91-plus figure or the 180 wounded here). Over 11,500 detained in the state of emergency and ANC and PAC banned. Confirms the course's 69 and the date; the 'at least 91' figure is a newer research claim not in Welsh, so cite it only to the web source and keep it labelled

Treason Trial 1956 to 1961: 156 accused, all eventually acquitted (course dates confirmed). Welsh says it was the last political trial with normal safeguards; Sabotage Act 1963 and 90-day detention, 180 days in 1965, indefinite detention under the Terrorism Act 1967

Welsh: by 1990 73 detainees had died in custody, including Biko in 1977; TRC recorded 5,002 torture instances reported by over 2,900 people; 131 people executed for political offences 1948 to 1990 per the Apartheid Museum plaque and 79 on death row in February 1990. Judiciary 'executive-minded' (TRC criticism). Detail for the lesson on TRC and sources

Verwoerd assassinated 06/09/1966; Vorster's pragmatism (apartheid a 'method' to preserve Afrikaner identity) and the verligte/verkrampte split; HNP defeated in 1970. 1968-9 and 1966-7 white-elite surveys: about two-thirds favoured rigid legal segregation, 91 per cent said democracy was 'not practicable'. In 1970 52 per cent of Africans lived in 'white' areas, so separate development was visibly failing (Vorster's 'magic 1978' reversal never came). Supports a 'internal contradictions' cause in lesson 4

Economic contradictions (Welsh): Africans were 69 per cent of the labour force in 1970; by 1977 white skill shortages (9,000 professional, 9,000 artisans); 90 per cent of exemption applications from African-labour limits granted in 1977; of 28 job-reservation determinations only three remained in 1979 (mining colour bars lasted to 1990). The 1973 Durban strikes (over 67,000 African workers) led to the Wiehahn Commission (1977, reports 1979 to 1980) and recognition of African unions. Welsh doubts the neo-Marxist claim that apartheid was simply functional to capitalism. Adds an 'economic pressure' cause that is internal, not only sanctions, to lesson 4

Information Scandal (1978): Department of Information spent about R80 million on covert propaganda including a front newspaper, The Citizen; Vorster resigned as PM 27/09/1978 and as State President June 1979; PW Botha won the leadership vote 98 to 74 over Mulder. Welsh's point: it eroded Afrikaner trust in leaders (a cause of internal erosion). Soweto aftermath: 10/08/1976 Cabinet minutes say Black Consciousness 'must be broken' and police could act more drastically 'which would cause more deaths'; Biko killed in September 1977; 18 mostly BC organisations banned October 1977. Hanf surveys 1974 and 1977 show better-educated whites more open to change

Course lesson 2: 'Defiance Campaign (1952), the Freedom Charter (1955) and the Treason Trial (1956 to 1961)'. Welsh gives more: Defiance Campaign launched 26/06/1952 with 8,500 volunteers arrested, riots left about 40 dead and the ANC called it off; Mandela says ANC membership rose from under 7,000 to about 100,000. Freedom Charter adopted June 1955 at Kliptown by nearly 3,000 delegates (ratified by the ANC in 1956); how far it reflected popular demands is disputed (Rusty Bernstein says the submitted papers were lost). Treason Trial: 156 arrested December 1956 (105 African, 21 Indian, 23 white, 7 Coloured); charges dropped against many, and the final 30 were acquitted in March 1961. Welsh's chapter 3 sentence that all 156 were acquitted is loose; the exact wording is that the final 30 were acquitted

Intra-black divisions: Durban African-Indian riots of January 1949 (142 dead: 87 African, 50 Indian); Africanist breakaway 1958 and PAC 1959 (Sobukwe) opposed the Charter's 'South Africa belongs to all who live in it'; Luthuli President-General from 1952. Good for the resistance lesson's 'not one movement' point, matching the Module 3 theme

Sharpeville (Welsh): 69 shot dead; crowd estimated from 3,000 to 25,000 (police said over 20,000); about 200 police inside the station; firing for some 20 seconds without an order; 'allegedly 52 of those killed were shot in the back' (course says 'many were shot in the back'). Welsh uses the official 69 and does not give the wounded count (course's 180 and the 91-plus revision come from the police record and web source, not this book). Date and the PAC role confirmed (PAC campaign 21/03/1960; Langa deaths three; State of Emergency 30/03/1960; 11,503 detained to August; ANC and PAC banned from 01/04/1960; pass laws suspended then reimposed 07/04/1960)

MK launched 16/12/1961 (a day sacred to Afrikaners, the Day of the Vow); Welsh notes police counted over 200 blasts by 1963; Operation Mayibuye 1963; Lilliesleaf farm at Rivonia. Course date of MK confirmed. Nearly 400,000 pass-law convictions in 1958. Luthuli won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1961 and accepted MK as an autonomous body

Mandela's detention: the course says the usual 27 years counts 'from his arrest in 1962, a date that the library does not give'. Welsh supplies it: Mandela was arrested on 5 August 1962 after 17 months underground (already imprisoned for incitement when police raided Lilliesleaf at Rivonia on 11/07/1963, 17 arrested). 05/08/1962 to 11/02/1990 is 27 years 6 months (our arithmetic), which resolves the course's [check current] note; sentence of life was passed on 12/06/1964 (date from the course, not from Welsh) so 25 years 8 months from sentence is also right

Rivonia: trial opened October 1963 with Mandela and nine others; after 86 days eight convicted and given life, Bernstein acquitted, Hepple's charges withdrawn (he fled). Welsh's chapter 3 summary (nine of ten convicted, seven life) disagrees with this chapter 4 account, which matches other sources: use eight life sentences. Judge de Wet declined the death penalty because the charge was sabotage, not treason. Mandela's dock speech (20/04/1964) ends with the 'prepared to die' sentence

Bantustans as political actors: Matanzima (Transkei), Buthelezi (KwaZulu; Inkatha founded 1975 after consultation with the ANC), Sebe (Ciskei held a 1981 referendum with 99 per cent yes on a 59.5 per cent poll though a survey found most opposed independence). Mandela: 'use the system' view vs Mbeki. Later Inkatha-ANC violence roots. Also ANC/SACP relationship: Soviet aid via SACP; Morogoro conference 1969 opened ANC to non-African members, NEC to non-Africans only after Kabwe 1985

Exile ANC 1960s to 1970s weak: MK had 'not fired a single shot on South African soil' by 1973 (Welsh quoting a source), Wankie campaign 1967, Hani memorandum. Popular stirring in the early 1970s owed more to Black Consciousness and independent labour than to the ANC: relevant to the 'why did apartheid end' lesson (internal mobilisation was not mainly the exiled ANC/MK)

Course: Biko's BC 'from the late 1960s, urged psychological liberation'. Welsh adds how: SASO formed 1969 after black students left Nusas; BC defined 'black' as anyone legally discriminated against as a unit (so Coloured and Indian included), a status and state of mind not a pigment; 'colonisation of the mind'; Biko excluded from medical school in 1971; Tiro's April 1972 graduation speech sparked a country-wide student boycott; eight SASO leaders including Biko banned in July 1973; SASO had about 6,000 members in 1973. Mandela and the SACP criticised BC as racialist or lacking class analysis. Add 2 to 3 sentences and the contrast to the course's lecturer lesson

Biko born 1946 in the Eastern Cape and killed by the security police in 1977 (Welsh, ch.7 and earlier); course's Biko dates confirmed; the course says he 'died in police custody on 12/09/1977' (date not in this chunk; check)

Course lesson 2: Hector Pieterson 'aged 12'. Welsh calls him a 'dying 13 year-old'. Sources differ on his age (12 or 13 are both in print); say 'aged 12 or 13' and name the disagreement instead of stating one age. Also Welsh: 15 people killed on 16/06/1976 including two schoolchildren in the first confrontation (course gives no first-day count); 48 police under Colonel Kleingeld, 40 of them black; marchers 10,000 to 15,000; first confrontation at Vilakazi Street; the Cillié Commission faulted police unpreparedness yet Welsh calls it a whitewash of police behaviour

Soweto causes in numbers: from 1974/75 a directive made Afrikaans and English equal media from Standard 5 (Social Studies and Mathematics in Afrikaans); 88.5 per cent of Soweto matric pupils' parents preferred English in a 1972 survey; secondary pupils 178,959 (1974) to 389,046 (1976); 257,505 enrolled in Form 1 in 1976 against Soweto capacity of 38,000; teacher:pupil 1:20 white vs 1:54 African in 1975; per capita R605 vs R39.53. Soweto population officially 650,000 (probably double). Treurnicht, deputy minister, said in May 1976 no real problem. The language rule was the fuse of wider grievances. Add numbers to lesson 2 and the uprising sequence

KEY CHECK. Course lesson 2: 'The official toll of the Cillie Commission was 176. Independent estimates for the months of unrest are higher, about 700'. Welsh: according to the Cillie Report 575 people were killed in the period 16/06/1976 to 28/02/1977 (country-wide, not only Soweto), and another 111 in 1977; many residents believed even 575 an undercount but 'no authoritative higher figure could be produced'; Ntatho Motlana of the Black Parents' Association said children 'died by their thousands' and doubted government figures. Welsh does not give 176 or 700. So the course's attribution of 176 to the Cillie Commission and the 'about 700' independent estimate cannot be checked in Welsh, and the Commission's own total in Welsh is 575. Fix: state 575 (Cillie, to 28/02/1977, with 111 more in 1977) as Welsh's figure; keep 176 only as a lower figure for the early Soweto phase attributed to officials in other sources [unverified here], and tag the whole as ESTIMATE/CONTESTED. Also 15 killed on the first day (16/06/1976)

Welsh: Biko murdered by security police on 12/09/1977 and 18 BC organisations banned a month later (October 1977); Black Parents' Association banned October 1977; at least 4,000 youths fled the country and MK gained about 3,000 recruits by end 1978; ANC had about 50 formal underground units (200 people) in 1976-7. Confirms Biko date and the Soweto-to-armed-struggle link
The dual-medium (Afrikaans) rule was withdrawn on 06/07/1976 by M. C. Botha: principals could choose the medium, a rare government retreat. Add to lesson 2 as the immediate result of Soweto

Welsh's thesis, stated in ch.6: 'a weakening of the resolve to maintain apartheid' within Afrikaner nationalism was a significant factor opening the way to negotiated transition, alongside black mobilisation. The course's four-cause table (resistance, economy, Cold War, elite negotiation) lacks this fifth cause: erosion of Afrikaner cohesion and confidence (embourgeoisement, press and writers, verligte/verkrampte split, Information Scandal). African population growth 3 per cent a year 1970-80, nearly double whites. Add as a fifth row in lesson 4 and tag [CONTESTED]; Welsh's own claim is that it is one factor, not the sole one

Church and apartheid: Cottesloe consultation (December 1960) condemned job reservation and migrant labour but the NGK synods repudiated it; Beyers Naude defrocked 1963, Christian Institute banned 1977; the NGK 1974 report Ras, Volk en Nasie defended apartheid; World Alliance of Reformed Churches suspended the NGK and NHK in 1982 (Boesak); in 1986 the NGK's Church and Society called apartheid unjustifiable and conservatives formed the Afrikaanse Protestantse Kerk (about 40,000 members). Material for a table in lesson 4 on Afrikaner institutions turning; the Conservative Party split from the NP in 1982 (Treurnicht)

Afrikaner embourgeoisement in numbers: white-collar share of Afrikaners 27.5 per cent (1936) to 66.2 per cent (1991); farming 41.2 per cent to 4.7 per cent; Afrikaner-controlled private sector share 9.6 per cent (1948-9) to 20.8 per cent (1975). Business contacts with the ANC: Gavin Relly's delegation met Tambo in Zambia in 1985; Broederbond chairman Pieter de Lange met Thabo Mbeki secretly in New York in 1986; Broederbond membership about 13,000 by mid-1980s. Business and Afrikaner elites were moving toward talks before 1990 (relevant to 'elite negotiation' cause)

Broederbond's 1986 paper 'Basic political conditions for the survival of the Afrikaner' (approved Nov 1986; 89 per cent of branches agreed) abandoned entrenched white rule and discriminatory laws, but kept group rights and power-sharing. Economy: GDP growth minus 1.2 per cent in 1985, zero in 1986. White conscription 1967, two years by 1977; the Border War and Vrye Weekblad (first issue November 1988) and Voelvry tour 1989 as cultural erosion (Grundlingh: effect limited, mainly white middle class). Afrikaner per-capita income ratio to English-speakers 47.8:100 in 1946 to nearly 70:100 in 1970

Course lesson 1 lists 'pass laws, various' without an end. Welsh: influx control (the pass laws, Section 10) was abolished in 1986 by PW Botha after a President's Council committee found it unworkable (over 200,000 arrests a year on average 1980 to 1985; 202,000 squatters at Crossroads). Mixed Marriages Act and section 16 of the Immorality Act repealed 1985. African unions recognised by 1979 legislation after Wiehahn. PW Botha PM from 28/09/1978; the 'adapt or die' speech July 1979; his 'reforms' were bounded by group rights (neo-apartheid). Add the reform timeline to lesson 3 or 4

Tricameral Constitution: referendum of white voters 02/11/1983; houses of 178 whites, 80 Coloured, 40 Indian, Africans excluded; 'own' versus 'general' affairs; Slabbert called it 'co-optive domination'. Conservative Party founded 20/03/1982 after Treurnicht's 22 dissidents lost the caucus vote 100 to 22. The course never mentions the Tricameral Parliament; it is the trigger for the UDF (1983) so add one sentence in lesson 3 and the UDF row. White real income per head fell 4.4 per cent 1975-80 while African income rose 3.3 per cent

Tricameral figures: November 1983 white referendum 76 per cent turnout, nearly 66 per cent yes; Coloured House poll 30.9 per cent, Indian House poll 20.29 per cent. Welsh: exclusion of Africans from the Tricameral Parliament provoked 'more than any other single factor' the forces that brought apartheid down (an unintended consequence: UDF formed 1983). Rubicon speech 15/08/1985 (Botha refused major reform; rand fell to 34 US cents on 28/08/1985); Commonwealth Eminent Persons Group mission wrecked by SADF raids on Gaborone, Harare, Lusaka on 19/05/1986. Both are triggers for the 1986 US sanctions in lesson 3

Course lesson 3: 'States of emergency from 1985 brought mass detention'. Welsh: a partial state of emergency from July 1985 (36, later 44 districts), then nationwide from June 1986, lasting until 1990; over 3,500 detained 1986-7; UDF and 16 affiliates banned and Cosatu restricted in February 1988. Political violence killed an estimated 2,681 people from September 1984 to end 1987; in 1986 about 50 per cent of deaths were conflict within black communities and over 30 per cent by security forces (SAIRR). 14 killed on 03/09/1984 (start of the 1984 revolt over rents), 149 by year-end per Welsh (175 for the year in total)

'Ripeness' argument for negotiation: Welsh (quoting de Klerk and noting Obasanjo's remark to Tambo) says talks became possible only when both sides saw neither could win on its own terms; the state of emergency taught revolutionaries by 1988 that there would be no quick victory. Useful for the 'why did it end' lesson: mutual stalemate rather than any single cause

Course lesson 4 row 'Economic pressure and sanctions: US sanctions of 1986; capital flight; cost of defence; weakness: sanctions' effect is hard to isolate'. Welsh agrees and goes further: GDP growth averaged 5.5 per cent a year in the 1960s, 3.25 per cent in the 1970s and 2.24 per cent in the 1980s; defence took 14.7 per cent of the budget in 1987-8; Savage and Lewis put the cost of apartheid at R56 billion in 1985 and 1987 GDP about 45 per cent lower than the 1946-75 trend (their counterfactuals); trade sanctions and disinvestment weakened the economy, but the oil embargo was 'largely circumvented' (cost R80 billion since 1979) and Welsh judges that sanctions were never likely on their own to force Botha to the table; many firms sold to local buyers at discounts. Use as the 'economy' evidence with sanctions' limits

Security-force violence: death squads (Vlakplaas, Eugene de Kock sentenced 1996 to two life terms plus 212 years; CCB set up 1986; Harms Commission 1990). TRC found security forces turned to extra-judicial killing as unrest rose. Unemployment 1987 estimates from 1.5 million to 6.1 million; 25 per cent of metropolitan Africans unemployed (Market Research Africa). De Klerk told the British ambassador in April 1987 that South Africa should not leave negotiation 'too late' as Rhodesia had; Niel Barnard's NIS advised from the early 1980s that there was no answer in fighting it out

Course lesson 4 names 'US sanctions of 1986; capital flight; cost of defence' as economic evidence. Welsh says 'far more significant than any of the sanctions' was the debt standstill started by Chase Manhattan in July 1985 (maturing loans called, new lending cut; R60 billion owed, R34 billion short-term), which forced South Africa to export capital and limit growth to about 2 per cent while the African population grew 2.7 per cent; domestic capital flight (direct investment abroad up 105.2 per cent in real terms 1980-85) may have exceeded disinvestment. Add the 1985 debt standstill to the sanctions row

The sanctions debate (for 'present both positions'): Anthony Sampson claimed international pressure and sanctions brought down apartheid; de Klerk said sanctions 'did more to delay the process of transformation than advance it' though costing about 1.5 per cent of annual growth in the 1980s and early 1990s; surveys (SAIIA 1986 and 1988; IRRC 1989) show sanctions hardened white attitudes and helped the Conservative Party (27 per cent in 1987, 31 per cent in 1989 election votes). Black opinion on sanctions was ambivalent because of job losses; Tutu and Cosatu supported them, Buthelezi opposed. Relly's September 1985 Zambia meeting with Tambo, Mbeki, Hani, Maharaj; Anglo American 'High Road, Low Road' scenarios shown to 230 groups. Welsh rejects the claim that business or capital drove NP policy (Schlemmer)

De Klerk became NP leader on 02/02/1989 vote (69 to 61 over Barend du Plessis) after Botha's stroke of 18/01/1989, and State President after Botha's forced resignation on 14/08/1989; 06/09/1989 election the NP fell to 93 seats and below 50 per cent of votes, Conservative Party 39 seats, Democratic Party 33. Course lesson 3 'F. W. de Klerk legalised the ANC ... on 02/02/1990' is right but omits his 1989 rise; add. Welsh: Botha's 1982 purge of the right 'without which the transition would almost certainly have been far more protracted and even bloodier'

Welsh's own answer to 'why did apartheid end' (opening of ch.8): the transition began 'when the leaderships of the contending forces recognised that the conflict was deadlocked' - neither could win; the process was 'the hardening of black resolve and the weakening of white resolve' while the security apparatus stayed strong. Armed struggle: MK was in military terms 'little more than an irritant' (about 1,200 guerrilla attacks 1976-89; about 12,000 trained by 1987) though it channelled support to the ANC and heightened white resistance; Mandela told himself in 1985 that 'a military victory was a distant if not impossible dream'. Evidence against a single cause; supports a 'stalemate' row in lesson 4 and corrects any claim that MK defeated the state. Also MK camp abuses (TRC found torture of suspected agents and mutineers); Operation Vula (1986)

'Black leverage' in numbers (Welsh ch.8): African population about 11 million (1960) to nearly 25 million (1985), over 40 per cent in 'white' areas; Africans in Standard 10: 835 (1960) to over 107,000 (1985); African union membership about 3 per cent of workers (1972) to at least 30 per cent (1988); strike man-days about 6 million in 1987 against 10,558 in 1978; Africans 32 per cent of personal disposable income in 1985. Unofficial estimate of 32,000 detained under emergency regulations June 1985 to September 1988; 406 'necklace' killings Sept 1984 to Dec 1989 (police statistics); Cosas founded 1979, banned August 1985; school boycotts 1984 (about 400,000 pupils in the 5 to 6 November stay-away). Worked-example material for lesson 3/4; handle necklacing with care (never condoned by UDF/ANC but their condemnation was slow)

UDF 1983 confirmed: Boesak's call in January 1983, launch at a Cape Town rally in August 1983, banned February 1988; claimed 700-800 affiliates and 2.5 million members (a claim; it was a federation, not individual membership). Sebokeng (Vaal) revolt began 03/09/1984 with 14 killed on day one (Welsh) after a rent rise of R5.90; 72 killed in the Vaal Triangle to 01/01/1985 (Vaal Ministers Solidarity Group); Uitenhage March 1985: 20 killed at a funeral procession (Kannemeyer inquiry). Welsh: the Tricameral Constitution 'spawned the UDF, which in turn precipitated the long crisis that was instrumental in eventually causing the downfall of apartheid'; 70 stayaways by June 1988

Nationwide state of emergency declared 12/06/1986 with over 30,000 troops in townships; state figures said unrest incidents fell 85 per cent and deaths 82 per cent in the next 12 months; over 27,000 detained in 1986. Yet Welsh: the UDF's 'politics of refusal' destroyed Botha's constitutional plan and was 'arguably the biggest single force behind the making of the deadlock' from which the transition emerged; the UDF was only 'in some measure' an ANC surrogate (Mandela). 'Ungovernability' and 'people's power' (people's courts, street committees) were the ANC/UDF slogans; Delmas treason trial 1985-88 (convictions overturned on appeal). Rent boycotts hit about 50 townships by September 1986. State kept control throughout, so the revolt did not 'topple' the state - a limit to any 'people power won' reading

Political violence totals: over 21,500 killed September 1984 to 1994, of whom roughly 3,000 by security forces and about 18,500 in internecine violence, mostly in Natal (Welsh, estimates). Necklacing nearly 400 plus 395 other burnings 1984-89. UDF-Azapo clashes killed possibly over 200; witdoeke attacks in Cape Town in May 1986 killed 44 and destroyed 60,000 shacks. Lesson 3/4 should say the revolt and its repression were both lethal and that most deaths in 1984-94 were not by the state: a balanced figure for the 'costs' discussion, flagged ESTIMATE. Also note: Welsh gives the 1973 Durban strikes as 'over 67,000' in ch.5 but 'over 61,000 in nearly 150 companies' in ch.8: use 'more than 60,000' and flag the discrepancy

COSATU formed November 1985 (course: 'COSATU, 1985' confirmed) with nearly 450,000 members, 721,000 by 1987 and 1.26 million by 1991; Cyril Ramaphosa led the NUM (100,000 members). August 1987 miners' strike: three weeks, 220,000 to 330,000 miners, 50,000 dismissed, about 30 deaths. Cosatu restricted February 1988; Mass Democratic Movement 1988-89; seven ANC prisoners (Sisulu, Mhlaba, Mlangeni and others) freed unconditionally in October 1989; strikes involving black workers: 207 (1980) to 1,148 (1987)

Inkatha-ANC/UDF conflict (the course never covers it, though it matters for 1990-94): Welsh counts over 10,700 deaths in KwaZulu-Natal 1976 to 1994, nearly 90 per cent between 1989 and 1994, plus several hundred more in the Transvaal; Inkatha revived 1975 with ANC support, rift after October 1979 London meeting; Inkatha claimed 1 million members by 1985; Welsh blames all three: Inkatha, the UDF/ANC and state security elements ('none did enough to end it'). Natal Indaba 1986 power-sharing proposal rejected by the NP. Needed for the 1990-94 negotiation section (Boipatong, violence) of lesson 3

Welsh's end-of-decade summary: by 1989 'the contending forces were deadlocked': the state too strong to be overthrown, ungovernability not achieved widely, seizure of power unrealistic. TRC found security forces collaborated with Inkatha against the UDF (warning, arming, transporting attackers); Welsh thinks the TRC underplayed the UDF's ungovernability campaign and Inkatha's fears. Buthelezi refused homeland independence for KwaZulu (saving over six million Zulu from losing citizenship): even de Klerk and Mandela credited this. Balanced-source example: the TRC is itself a source with a perspective

Course row 'End of the Cold War: communist threat justification weakened in 1989; weakness: talks began before the Cold War's end'. Welsh agrees on both halves: secret contacts began earlier (Coetsee visited Mandela in hospital August 1985; Barnard's NIS team talked to Mandela from May 1988; Botha met Mandela 05/07/1989; de Klerk first met him 13/12/1989) but the fall of the Berlin Wall (09/11/1989) and Soviet retreat (Namibia's independence March 1990) 'created an opportunity for a much more adventurous approach'. De Klerk himself says his 'quantum leap' came in 1985-86, not 1989. Whites' attitudes: in 1988 nearly 62 per cent opposed talks with the ANC (78.5 per cent of Afrikaans-speakers); a February 1990 poll found 44 per cent of all whites supported unbanning the ANC, PAC and SACP

Back-channel talks before 1990: Stellenbosch professors Esterhuyse and Terreblanche with Willem de Klerk met ANC figures a dozen times 1987-90; Slabbert's Dakar meeting with the ANC in June 1987 (60 mostly Afrikaners); Richard Rosenthal shuttle between Mbeki and Stoffel van der Merwe. De Klerk's four options (1988) and choice of fundamental change with minority protection; on taking office he abolished the National Security Management System and downgraded the State Security Council (restoring cabinet government). 1989 election: Conservative Party 31.2 per cent of the vote (about 680,000) against 1.03 million for the NP. For lesson 3: the 02/02/1990 announcement followed years of secret contact and was prepared by de Klerk's 1989 moves; his 'quantum leap' announcement came 'all at once' to seize the initiative

Mandela's route to talks: Botha's sixth release offer (early 1985) refused with the message 'Only free men can negotiate. Prisoners cannot enter into contracts' (read by his daughter, 10/02/1985); April 1982 transfer to Pollsmoor; secret Coetsee meetings from 1985-86 without telling colleagues (Kathrada opposed, Sisulu lukewarm). Local negotiations (civics, unions) taught both sides negotiation; Mbeki's contacts with about 70 visiting groups; Valli Moosa's view that there was a stalemate. Use for the 'ripening / stalemate' lesson and the Mandela's primary-voice table (statement from the dock vs. his 1985 refusal)

Two new primary documents for lesson 5 (reading apartheid sources): Mandela's March 1989 memorandum to Botha (handed over at the 05/07/1989 meeting; Welsh calls it 'one of the seminal documents') and the ANC's Harare Declaration of 21/08/1989 (released through the OAU; demanded release of prisoners, unbanning, troops out of townships, end of the emergency, then a ceasefire, interim government and a new constitution). Also the December 1988 Angola-Cuba-South Africa agreement behind Namibian independence. Welsh: the ANC was deeply divided on negotiation; 'who would blink first'

Course lesson 3: 'F. W. de Klerk legalised the ANC and PAC on 02/02/1990'. Welsh: the 02/02/1990 speech also unbanned the SACP and 'a number of subsidiary organisations', lifted emergency restrictions on 33 organisations (including the UDF and Cosatu), limited emergency detention to six months, and announced Mandela's unconditional release (done 11/02/1990, aged 71, after the date was pushed back so Mandela's thunder was not stolen). Add the SACP and the wider scope. Also Groote Schuur talks 2-4 May 1990 (first government-ANC meeting; Slovo included); Operation Vula discovered July 1990; 3,699 political-violence deaths in 1990 (up 163 per cent; 1,811 in Natal)

1990-91 steps not in the course: Pretoria Minute 06/08/1990 (ANC suspends armed struggle; Slovo proposed it, about 98 per cent of supporters thought it a sellout per Slovo); DF Malan Accord 12/02/1991 (ANC to refrain from attacks, infiltration, underground structures); UDF dissolved 1991; Cosatu-ANC-SACP 'Triple Alliance' May 1990; Ventersdorp clash 09/08/1991. 1990 was 'the most violent year in modern South African history' (Welsh); surveys: 52.3 per cent of whites favoured talks with ANC in Jan 1990 (36.2 per cent in 1988); 74.5 per cent of a July 1990 sample supported ANC-NP talks. Chris Hani assassinated 10/04/1993 by two extremists (course gives April 1993: confirmed). 'Third force' security elements: ANC and de Klerk blamed each other; Welsh calls the truth more complex

Violence during negotiation (for lesson 3's 1990-94 paragraph): countrywide political-violence deaths per Welsh: 1991 2,706 (2,510 in a later passage), 1992 3,347, 1993 3,794 (3,706 later), 1994 2,434; KwaZulu-Natal 1,684 / 1,427 / 1,489 / 1,464. Welsh's own two sets disagree slightly, so quote 'about 2,500 to 2,700' and 'about 3,700 to 3,800' with ESTIMATE. Inkathagate (July 1991: state money to Inkatha, R250,000, and Uwusa, R1.5 million; SADF trained 200 KwaZulu police in 1986); de Klerk ended 41 secret projects; Harms Commission (1990) failed against the CCB. Mandela-Buthelezi Durban accord 29/01/1991 (over 8,000 dead by then). Political-prisoner dispute: ANC claimed about 5,000, de Klerk fewer than 200; Norgaard principles for 'political offences'

Repeal of the pillars (course never states when): the 1913 and 1936 land laws (13.7 per cent of the country to Africans), the Group Areas Act, the Reservation of Separate Amenities Act and the Population Registration Act were repealed in 1990-91 (de Klerk, per Welsh); NP opened to all races end of 1990. White referendum on continuing talks 17/03/1992 followed Conservative by-election gains. National Peace Accord September 1991 and Goldstone Commission; Mandela April 1993 speech admitting ANC members were killing people. Add a one-line dismantling timeline to lesson 1/3: 1985 mixed marriage laws, 1986 pass laws, 1990-91 land, group areas, population registration

National Peace Accord signed September 1991 by 29 organisations (not the CP, AWB; PAC and Azapo declined); Goldstone Commission. Welsh frames 1985-91 with Zartman's 'hurting stalemate' / 'prenegotiation' theory: this is Welsh's analytic spine for lesson 4 (conflict ripens when both sides see costs of no deal exceed those of a deal)

Constitutional positions before CODESA: ANC Constitutional Guidelines 1988 (majority rule, unitary state); NP's September 1991 model (rotating three-party presidency, regional second house; Slovo mocked it as a 'House of Losers'); IFP federalism. Government polls in the late 1980s predicted the ANC would win about 60 per cent: the 1994 result (62.65 per cent) matched, which supports the course's 62.65 figure and shows the NP knew its minority position. Welsh's point: the 'sufficient consensus' compromise and power-sharing for five years (GNU) lowered the stakes of the first election

Course lesson 3: 'The CODESA negotiations of 1991 to 1993 were interrupted by violence ...'. Welsh's dates: CODESA opened 20/12/1991 with 19 parties at the World Trade Centre (PAC and Conservative Party absent); Working Groups from 20/01/1992; the white referendum 17/03/1992; the opening-day de Klerk-Mandela row ('illegitimate minority regime'); de Klerk's two-phase proposal (interim constitution then elected constitution-making body bound by agreed principles and certified by a Constitutional Court) was the key compromise. So CODESA itself ran from December 1991 to mid-1992 (Codesa 2 collapse May 1992; later the Multiparty Negotiating Process 1993): say 'the CODESA talks of 1991 to 1992 and the multiparty process of 1993'; Ramaphosa-Meyer back channel

White referendum 17/03/1992 (question: continue the reform process begun on 02/02/1990): 68.7 per cent yes on an 85 per cent poll; only one of 15 regions (Pietersburg) voted no; estimated 79 per cent of English-speakers yes, 38 per cent of Afrikaans-speakers no (forecasts had been 53-55 per cent). It gave de Klerk an 'unambiguous mandate' and ended the need to return to white voters. CODESA's Working Group 2 collapsed on 15/05/1992 over voting majorities (NP 70/75 per cent vs ANC two-thirds); Ramaphosa deliberately engineered it; then the Leipzig-option mass action. Good for lesson 3's negotiation timeline and the 'elite pact' cause (the ANC accepted power-sharing for five years)

Boipatong massacre 17/06/1992 (course: 'June 1992'): 45 killed and 22 injured by KwaMadala hostel dwellers (IFP supporters). Source conflict worth showing in lesson 5: the ANC and TRC (1998) alleged police collusion; Goldstone Commission with Bhagwati and Waddington, the 1994 trial judge and the TRC amnesty committee (2000) found no evidence of police involvement, though Waddington criticised the police investigation. Welsh credits Anthea Jeffery's critique of the TRC findings. Also Bisho massacre 07/09/1992 (29 ANC marchers killed by Ciskei soldiers; Goldstone also criticised the ANC); Record of Understanding 26/09/1992; Derek Keys's 'dirty pictures' economic briefing (August 1992) moved the ANC off nationalisation. Good case of weighing a commission's finding (TRC) against courts

Elite compromise detail for lesson 4 ('Elite negotiation' row; weakness 'critics argue economic power stayed with the old elite'): Joe Slovo's 1992 'sunset clause' paper (time-limited power-sharing, job guarantees for civil servants and security forces) accepted by the ANC NEC on 25/11/1992; Record of Understanding 26/09/1992 (elected constitution-making body, interim GNU); Meyer says the ANC 'caved' less than Slovo claimed (constitutional continuity, rights, property rights). Radical critics (Pallo Jordan) said the compromise capitulated to the regime. So the course's elite-negotiation weakness is a real contemporary criticism, not only a later one. Buthelezi's COSAG formed 06/10/1992 and a near-secessionist KwaZulu draft 01/12/1992

Lesson 5 source-criticism of the TRC (course says it is 'not a court' and 'praised for exposing truth, criticised for limited reparations'). Welsh adds specific, contested criticisms: none of the 15 commissioners (1998) came from NP or IFP backgrounds, many staff were sympathetic to the liberation movement; Tutu and Boraine commented adversely on de Klerk's evidence the day after he testified (14/05/1997) and later apologised after a court action; de Klerk obtained a court order removing a finding about him from the report in 1998. Counter-view (Boraine, de Kock): de Klerk 'turned a blind eye'. Goldstone Commission revelations of 16/11/1992 about a 'third force' (Military Intelligence's Directorate of Covert Collection); Steyn's investigation led to 23 officers dismissed in December 1992 ('Night of the Generals'). Present both views, labelled as Welsh's assessment

Chris Hani shot dead 10/04/1993 (aged 51) at Boksburg by Janusz Waluz, with Clive Derby-Lewis; about 70 deaths in rioting, 120,000 at his funeral on 19/04/1993; the Multiparty Negotiating Process opened 01/04/1993 with 26 organisations; election date 27/04/1994 agreed on 01/06/1993; Interim Constitution agreed 25-28/10/1993 and ratified by the MPNP on 18/11/1993. Confirms the course's lesson 3 dates ('Hani April 1993; interim constitution 1993'). Welsh: the NP's bargaining power fell from mid-1992; 'sufficient consensus' meant ANC plus NP agreement (Ramaphosa's blunt gloss alienated the IFP). PAC/Apla attacks on whites (St James Church 25/07/1993)

Interim Constitution adopted by the MPNP on 18/11/1993 and ratified by Parliament on 22/12/1993; Transitional Executive Council (from December 1993) with IEC and Independent Media Commission; 34 constitutional principles that the final constitution must meet (Constitutional Court certification); nine provinces. Risk of ultra-right war: General Constand Viljoen (Afrikaner Volksfront) chose to join the election rather than lead a revolt (met Mandela from August 1993); Meiring told him the SADF would stop a coup. This is the 'civil war averted' context for lesson 3's 'how it ended' and the weighing of the people who made the settlement hold

Run-up to 27/04/1994: Battle of Bop 11/03/1994 (about 60 killed; the SADF removed Mangope and Viljoen's force withdrew); Viljoen registered the Freedom Front; Shell House shooting 28/03/1994 (53 IFP marchers killed); state of emergency in Natal 31/03/1994; Kissinger-Carrington mediation failed (Kissinger: the date is 'a poison tree'); IFP agreed to enter the election on 19/04/1994 (Okumu mediation) - eight days before the vote; AWB car bombs killed 21 in the week before the election. Core point: the transition nearly failed on both flanks, and the SADF held to civilian control. Useful for lesson 3 sequence and for 'why not civil war'

The 'elite pact' / economic trade-off in Welsh's words: the ANC got relatively unfettered majority rule; whites kept domination of the private sector, subject to redress (affirmative action, land restitution, empowerment). 'Like an inarticulate major premise' the trade was never stated publicly. A radical critic (cited by Welsh) called the outcome capitulation to business. Interim Constitution property clause (s28) allowed expropriation for public purposes with compensation 'just and equitable' including market value; land restitution for dispossession since 1913 was not covered (13.7 per cent). GNU: parties with 80 of 400 seats could nominate an executive deputy president; 5 per cent of the vote entitled a party to Cabinet seats. Direct material for the lesson 4 'elite negotiation' row and for balancing 'weakness: economic power stayed with the old elite' with Welsh's view that the ANC gave up less than critics claim

1994 election confirmed by Welsh: ANC 62.65 per cent and 252 of 400 seats (short of two-thirds; Mandela was relieved), NP 20.6 per cent, IFP 10.54 per cent (43 seats; it won KwaZulu-Natal 50.3 per cent against ANC 32.2 per cent), Freedom Front 2.17 per cent, DP 1.73, PAC 1.25. Voting ran 26 to 29 April 1994 (main day 27/04/1994), de Klerk conceded on 02/05/1994, final result announced 06/05/1994. Welsh calls the election 'more a rite of passage' than a fully free and fair contest: 165 no-go zones, temporary voter cards (over 3.5 million issued), unreconcilable ballots; de Klerk believed up to a million illegal votes; Mandela declined to challenge the KZN result. 94 per cent of ANC votes came from Africans; over 60 per cent of Coloured and Indian voters backed the NP. Add the dates 26-29 April / 06 May and the 'flawed but accepted' point to lesson 3

Conclusion confirms the KEY Soweto check: 'the official figure for the number of deaths occurring in the Soweto Uprising of 1976 and its (countrywide) aftermath is 575; many, notably Sowetans, believe the actual figure to be much higher'. The course's 'official toll of the Cillie Commission was 176; independent about 700' therefore misattributes the official number and its scope. Fix lesson 2 and the take-away: official 575 (countrywide, 16/06/1976 to 28/02/1977, per Welsh); 176 and 700 appear in other sources and must be labelled as such [not checked in Welsh]

Welsh's answer to 'why did apartheid end' (his own ranking): no single cause; 'the transition occurred because the principal antagonists, the ANC and the NP, mutually recognised that neither could win ... the conflict was deadlocked'; shifts in the black and white blocs and international isolation explain the stalemate; leadership (Mandela, de Klerk) the 'indispensable complement'; Garton Ash's 'refolution' (change from above and below). On the economy: three views (liberal 'capitalism erodes apartheid', Marxist 'capitalism and apartheid symbiotic', Blumer 'outside factors'); Welsh sides with Lipton's case that capitalists did not want apartheid and lacked the power to remove it, and says the indirect effects of growth (urbanisation, skilled African labour, unions) were the main erosive effect; de Klerk: growth 'a far more powerful agent for change than sanctions'. Rank of Welsh's causes for lesson 4: (1) stalemate recognised by leaders, (2) mass mobilisation and unions, (3) economic and demographic pressure, (4) Afrikaner erosion of resolve, with sanctions and Cold War end as facilitating. Tag [CONTESTED]

Death toll across apartheid (Welsh, estimates): about 23,000 political-conflict fatalities 1948 to 1994 (131 executions for political offences, 72 detention deaths here; ch.3 said 73 by 1990), of which about 21,561 between 1984 and 1994, 10,744 of them in KwaZulu-Natal, about 3,000 by the security forces; excludes regional wars (EPG accepted a figure of 100,000 credible). African population nearly trebled under apartheid; life expectancy 63 by 1990. Welsh also says Mbeki's AIDS policy caused over 330,000 deaths (Harvard estimate) - not in scope, skip
